title: All will forget
hookLine: soon you'll forget everything, and soon everything will forget you (Meditations 7.21)

cards: Try naming all eight of your great-grandparents. Maybe one name comes, maybe a story about a farm or a ship.
These were people with whole lives: first loves, embarrassments, opinions about the neighbors, worries about what people thought of them.

Every one of those worries is gone now, and so are most of the people who could have remembered them. That can sound bleak. Marcus Aurelius treated it as a kind of relief, and he wrote it down in one short line.

teach.b: Meditations seven, twenty-one, in George Long's translation, is just this: "Near is thy forgetfulness of all things; and near the forgetfulness of thee by all." Two forgettings, facing each other.

Soon you'll forget everything; soon everything will forget you. This is an emperor, a man whose face was stamped on coins. If anyone could hope to be remembered, it was Marcus, and we do still know his name.
But the opinions of the people around him, the senators, the courtiers, the crowd, on any given Tuesday? Gone.
He uses the line as medicine for one sickness, worry about reputation, and he comes back to it again and again in the Meditations. What will they think? What will they say about me?

teach.h: WHAT'S LEFT: THE GOOD YOU DID.
teach.b: His answer isn't that people's opinions don't exist. It's that they're brief.
The ones who praise you will be forgotten, and so will the ones who mock you. A worry built on something that short shouldn't get to run your whole day.

On his view, if embarrassments are soon forgotten, much of the fear around them has nothing to stand on: the awkward thing you said in the meeting, the post that didn't land, the question you were afraid to ask.
What's left is whether you did good while you were here.

how: Readers of Marcus often use 7.21 when anxious about reputation, reminding themselves that both praise and embarrassment are soon forgotten, and turning back to what they can do well now.

o: a general whose name was erased after he died
a Roman ruler who built monuments so he'd be remembered
the emperor who said all will soon forget, and be forgotten

games.q: all will forget — tap the pairs.

s: Meditations 7.21 is a single short sentence
near is your forgetting of all things, and near all things' forgetting of you.
Marcus says other people's opinions don't exist
he says they're brief, so they shouldn't run your day.

games.q: you're afraid to ask a question in a meeting because you might look foolish. by 7.21, what's the move?
o: stay quiet to protect your reputation.
ask it; the embarrassment, if any, will soon be forgotten.
ask someone else to ask it for you.
games.why: Meditations 7.21: near is your forgetting of all things, and their forgetting of you. A worry that short shouldn't decide what you do.

practice: Hold one worry about how you look to others, a mistake at work, something you said, a fear of seeming foolish, and then look far ahead, long after you're gone, when nobody alive remembers it.
Let the worry sit in that long quiet and notice what's left as it shrinks. Let it go on an out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who wrote that you'll soon forget everything, and everything will soon forget you, as medicine for worrying what people think. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: forgetting. In myth, Lethe was the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.

carryVoice: Your line: two forgettings facing each other. Praise and mockery fade alike. Day five hundred eighty-nine, done.

sources.q: Near is thy forgetfulness of all things; and near the forgetfulness of thee by all.
